newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sony, Nintendo to lead game machine industry.
newsitem.headline: Sony, Nintendo to lead game machine industry.

text.p: Sony Corp and Nintendo Co Ltd are becoming the two dominating giants in the game machine market with Matsushita Electric Industrial Co Ltd seen pulling out of the development of a next-generation 64-bit game console, analysts said on Friday.

"Although Matsushita's pull-out has already been widely expected, it meant that Nintendo and Sony will continue to be the main competitors in the game industry for a while," said Akira Namekawa, analyst at Yamaichi Research Institute.

Matsushita Electric Industrial president Yoichi Morishita told reporters on Thursday in Osaka that the 64-bit machine currently being developed by the company will not be a pure game machine, but rather a terminal with various functions including games.
The company is now selling a 32-bit game machine which is struggling to the capture a significant share in the market.
Since its launch in the United States about four years ago, the game machine's total sales in the global market have so far only reached 1.38 million units
Sharply contrasting that performance is the extremely robust sales for the 32-bit game machine, PlayStation, sold by Sony Computer Entertainment Inc.

The firm has shipped out a total of 16 million PlayStations globally as of the end of May. The machine was first put on the Japanese market in December 1994. The company plans to sell 18 million units in the current business year to March 31, 1998.

Analysts said that the success of Sony, a late comer to the game machine market, lay in its emphasis on winning the support of third-party game software developers so that it can offer attractive games.
They also said Matsushita failed to win the hearts of game players because it did not have as much attractive software as its competitors.

Sony rival Nintendo introduced a 64-bit game machine, Nintendo 64, which is faster and smarter than 32-bit machines, last June. As of the end of March 1997, it sold 2.04 million machines in Japan and an additional 4.08 million overseas.
The company aims to sell 12 million units of Nintendo 64 globally in 1997/98 ending in March.
"Matsushita's case points out to the fact that it is not so easy for a home-appliances maker to simply enter the game machine business and succeed," a spokesman for Nintendo said.
Meanwhile, Sega Enterprises Ltd, once a dominant player in the market, is shifting its focus to the lucrative game software business from its loss-making game hardware.
A company official said earlier this week that the company does not plan to upgrade its Sega Saturn 32-bit game console.
